intro: About 1.2 billion people, roughly one in seven people on Earth, are Hindus. On any given morning, many of them light a lamp at a home shrine, offer a flower to an image of Ganesha or Krishna, or chant a verse older than any other scripture still in daily use. In the Chicago area, Hindu families worship at temples in Lemont, Aurora and beyond, shop for festival sweets on Devon Avenue, and take their children to weekend classes to learn the great stories.

Hinduism is hard to fit into the categories people often use for religion. It has no single founder, no single book and no central authority. It includes worshipers of Vishnu, of Shiva and of the Goddess, philosophers who speak of one ultimate reality, and poets who sing their love for a personal God. Its texts range from the ancient Vedas and Upanishads to the epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and the Bhagavad Gita, which Swami Vivekananda helped introduce to Americans in Chicago in 1893.

In this unit you will read those texts and the ideas they carry: Brahman and atman, samsara and karma, dharma and moksha. You will meet the many deities and the several paths Hindus describe, visit puja and festivals, and study the history and reform of caste. Then you will sit in Arjuna's chariot, follow Krishna's answer, and see how readers from Shankara to Gandhi have understood it. By the end you should be able to explain these ideas accurately, attribute them to the traditions that hold them, and compare readings fairly.
bigQuestion: How do Hindu traditions answer the question of how to live rightly in the world while seeking freedom from it?

chapters.title: The Vedas and the Many Paths
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one tradition hold many gods, many paths and many texts, and still be recognized as one family?

story.title: Lamps on a West Ridge Windowsill
story.kicker: On one autumn night, a row of small clay lamps turns an ordinary Chicago apartment into a place of welcome.
paragraphs: It is a cold evening in late October, a few blocks from Devon Avenue on Chicago's North Side. The sari shops and sweet shops along the avenue have been busy all week. Inside a second-floor apartment, a sophomore named Priya is kneeling by the front window with a box of matches. Her grandmother hands her small clay lamps, one at a time. Each lamp is a shallow dish of oil with a cotton wick. Priya lights them and sets them in a row along the sill.

The lamps are diyas, and tonight is Diwali, the festival of lights. Her grandmother explains, as she does every year, that the lights welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of good fortune, into a clean and bright home. Then she tells the other story too: how Prince Rama came home to the city of Ayodhya after fourteen years in exile, and how the people lit lamps to guide him. Priya has heard both stories since she was small. She asks which one is the real reason for the lamps.

Her grandmother laughs. In her family's village in Gujarat, she says, people told it one way. Her friend from Tamil Nadu tells it another way. Her neighbor downstairs, a Jain family, lights lamps tonight for a different teacher altogether, and Sikh families in the suburbs celebrate their own festival on the same night. The lights mean all of these things at once, she says. That is not a problem to solve. That is how it works.

On the small shelf by the kitchen, there is a home shrine. It holds a brass image of Ganesha with his elephant head, a picture of Krishna playing a flute, and a small lamp that is lit every morning. Priya's father will say a short prayer there before the family eats sweets and the younger cousins run outside with sparklers. The apartment smells of ghee, incense and fried dough.

Priya's question is a good place to begin studying Hinduism. Many religions trace themselves to one founder or one book. Hinduism has neither. It is a large family of traditions that grew in South Asia over more than three thousand years. It holds many texts, many forms of worship and many ways of naming the divine. This chapter follows the threads that tie that family together.
story.think: Priya's grandmother says a festival can have several meanings at once. What does that suggest about how to study a tradition with no single founder or book?

lessons.title: One Name, Many Paths
lessons.mainIdea: Hinduism is not one organization with one founder; it is a family of related traditions that grew in South Asia over thousands of years.
reading: Ask a Hindu in Chicago, in Mumbai and in Bali to describe their religion, and you may hear three different answers. One may speak mostly of the god Vishnu. Another may center her life on the goddess Durga. A third may talk about meditation and the self, with little mention of any deity. Scholars therefore describe *Hinduism* as a family of traditions, not a single church. It has no founder, no single sacred book and no central authority that speaks for everyone.

The word itself came from outside. Ancient Persians used the name of the Sindhu, the Indus River, for the people who lived beyond it. Over centuries, Hindu became a label for the people and traditions of India. Many Hindus prefer an older name from their own texts: *Sanatana Dharma*, often translated as the eternal way or the eternal order. The name suggests a truth that was not invented at one moment but has always been there.

What holds the family together? Most Hindus share certain things. They honor the Vedas as sacred, even if few read them. They share ideas such as karma, rebirth and dharma. They worship in homes and temples through offerings called puja. And they tell the same great stories, such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. Within that shared frame, the variety is enormous, and adherents often see that variety as a strength.

Today there are about 1.2 billion Hindus, according to common estimates. Most live in India, where Hindus make up roughly four in five people, and in Nepal. Large communities also live in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Indonesia's island of Bali, Mauritius, the Caribbean, Britain and the United States. The Chicago area is home to many Hindu families, temples and cultural centers.

lessons.title: The Vedas: Heard and Remembered
lessons.mainIdea: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures, hymns and rituals in Sanskrit that were memorized and passed down by mouth for centuries before they were written.
reading: Picture a boy in a traditional school in South India, sitting cross-legged in front of his teacher. The teacher chants a line in Sanskrit, and the boy repeats it exactly, with the same rise and fall of pitch. They do this for hours a day, for years. This is how the *Vedas* have been kept alive. For many centuries they were not written at all. They were memorized and chanted, with methods so careful that scholars think the wording changed very little.

The word Veda means knowledge. There are four Vedas: the Rig Veda, the Sama Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Atharva Veda. The oldest, the Rig Veda, holds more than a thousand hymns. Scholars date its earliest parts to roughly 1500 to 1200 BCE, though estimates vary. Many hymns praise deities of nature and ritual, such as Agni, the god of fire, and Indra, a god of storm and war. Priests chanted them at fire sacrifices.

Hindus divide their sacred texts into two kinds. The word *shruti* means what is heard. It refers to the Vedas, which many Hindus believe ancient seers heard or perceived rather than composed. The word *smriti* means what is remembered. It includes later texts written by human authors, such as the great epics, the law books and the Puranas. For many Hindus, shruti carries the highest authority, even though smriti texts are far more widely read.

Few Hindus today read the Vedas cover to cover. Yet Vedic verses are still chanted at weddings, at the thread ceremony that marks a boy's entry into study in some families, and at funerals. One famous verse, the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, is recited daily by many Hindus as a prayer for light and understanding.

lessons.title: The Upanishads: Brahman and Atman
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads teach that behind the changing world is one ultimate reality, Brahman, and that the deepest self, atman, is one with it.
reading: The *Upanishads* are later texts attached to the Vedas, many composed around 800 to 300 BCE. Their name suggests sitting down near a teacher. Many are dialogues, in which a student questions a teacher about the deepest things: What is real? What am I? What remains when everything changes? Because they come at the end of the Vedas, they are also called Vedanta, the end or goal of the Veda.

One famous scene appears in the Chandogya Upanishad. A father, Uddalaka, tells his son Shvetaketu to drop salt into a cup of water and come back the next morning. The salt has vanished from sight, but every sip tastes salty. So it is, the father says, with the subtle essence of the world. You cannot see it, yet it is in everything. Then he adds the line that later teachers made famous: you are that.

That essence is *Brahman*, the one ultimate reality behind all things. The self at the core of each person is called *atman*. The Upanishads teach that atman is not the body, the thoughts or the personality, which all change. Many passages hold that atman and Brahman are, at bottom, the same. To realize this truth is to be freed from ignorance.

Hindu thinkers have read these texts in different ways. The teacher Shankara, around the 8th century CE, taught Advaita, or non-dualism: atman and Brahman are one, and separateness is an illusion. Later teachers such as Ramanuja held that the soul is real and distinct but depends wholly on a personal God. Both schools claim the Upanishads as their source.

sections.title: The Wheel and the Way Out

lessons.title: Samsara and Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe the soul is reborn again and again in samsara, and that karma, the result of one's actions, shapes each new life.
reading: At a Hindu funeral, the body is usually cremated, and the family may later scatter the ashes in a river, ideally the Ganges. Mourners often say that the soul has moved on, not that it has ended. Many Hindus believe the atman sheds a body the way a person sheds worn-out clothes, then takes a new one. This round of birth, death and rebirth is called *samsara*, which means wandering or flowing on.

What decides the next life? The answer is *karma*. The word means action, and it also means the result that action brings. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, a teacher says that as a person acts, so that person becomes: good actions make one good, harmful actions make one harmful. Karma is not seen as reward and punishment handed out by a judge. Many Hindus describe it more like a law of nature, the way a seed grows into its own kind of plant.

Karma includes thoughts and intentions, not only deeds. It can shape the circumstances of a future life, and many believe it also shapes character in this life. Hindus do not all agree on every detail. Some stress that a gracious God can soften or remove karma. Others stress personal effort. But most agree that each person's choices matter, because they carry forward.

Samsara is not usually seen as a happy endless adventure. Even good rebirths end in death and more rebirth. For that reason, many Hindu texts describe samsara as something to be escaped. The next two lessons explain the ideas of right living and final release that answer this problem. Together, samsara, karma, dharma and moksha form a framework most Hindus share.

lessons.title: Dharma: Duty and Right Order
lessons.mainIdea: Dharma is the right way of living, the duty and moral order that fit a person's role, stage of life and community.
reading: A young woman in Chicago must decide whether to take a job across the country or stay near her aging parents. A Hindu grandmother might ask her a question: what is your *dharma* here? Dharma is one of the richest words in Hindu thought. It can mean duty, law, right conduct, religion and the order that holds the world together. In daily life, it usually means doing what is right for your role and situation.

Classical Hindu texts teach that dharma is not the same for everyone. A parent, a student, a ruler and a teacher each have different duties. Some texts also describe four stages of life, called ashramas: student, householder, forest dweller, who steps back from worldly life, and renunciant, who gives up possessions to seek release. Few Hindus today follow all four stages strictly, but the ideal of life as a journey with changing duties remains.

The same texts name four goals of life, the *purusharthas*. Dharma is right living. Artha is prosperity and success. Kama is pleasure, love and beauty. Moksha is final release from rebirth. The first three are seen as good when they are pursued within dharma. Wealth and love are not condemned, but they are meant to serve a well-ordered life.

Hindus also speak of general duties that apply to everyone, such as truthfulness, self-control and *ahimsa*, not harming living beings. Many Hindus are vegetarian partly because of ahimsa. When personal duty and general duty seem to clash, the question becomes hard. That is exactly the problem Arjuna faces in the Bhagavad Gita, as the next chapter shows.

lessons.title: Moksha: Release from the Wheel
lessons.mainIdea: Moksha is the final goal in much Hindu thought: freedom from the cycle of rebirth, understood in different ways by different schools.
reading: In the holy city of Varanasi, on the Ganges River, cremation fires burn day and night on stone steps called ghats. Many elderly Hindus travel there hoping to die in the city, because tradition holds that dying in Varanasi brings release. That release has a name: *moksha*, freedom from samsara. Moksha means liberation. It is the fourth and highest of the four goals of life.

What is moksha like? Hindu schools answer differently. In the Advaita tradition, moksha is the realization that atman and Brahman were always one, like a drop of water returning to the sea. In devotional traditions, moksha is often pictured as eternal loving closeness to a personal God, such as Vishnu or Shiva, while the soul remains itself. Both agree that moksha ends rebirth and suffering.

How does one reach moksha? Again, Hindus describe several ways, which later lessons call paths or yogas. Some stress knowledge and insight. Some stress devotion and the grace of God. Some stress selfless action. Some stress meditation. Many Hindus combine them. Most also believe that moksha may take many lifetimes, which is why living well now still matters.

Not every Hindu thinks about moksha daily. Many focus on good karma, family duty, worship and a good rebirth. Scholars sometimes note that the tradition holds both goals side by side: living well within the world, and seeking release from it. Each family and teacher balances the two in its own way.

lessons.title: Vishnu and His Avatars
lessons.mainIdea: Vishnu, the preserver, is worshiped by many Hindus as the supreme God who descends to earth in forms called avatars, including Rama and Krishna.
reading: In a Hindu temple in Aurora, west of Chicago, the central image shows a standing, dark-skinned figure crowned with gold. He is Venkateswara, a form of *Vishnu* widely worshiped in South India. Devotees line up to see him, a moment of worship called *darshan*, seeing and being seen by the deity. Worshipers of Vishnu are called Vaishnavas, and they form one of the largest groups of Hindus.

Hindu texts often describe three great functions of the divine: Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves and Shiva destroys so that renewal can come. Scholars call this grouping the Trimurti. In practice, few Hindus worship Brahma, and many see either Vishnu or Shiva as the supreme God who performs all three roles.

Vaishnavas believe that when goodness weakens and evil grows, Vishnu descends to earth to restore order. Each descent is an *avatar*. Tradition often lists ten, including a fish, a boar and a man-lion. The two most beloved are Rama, the ideal king of the Ramayana, and Krishna, the divine teacher of the Bhagavad Gita and the playful cowherd of many stories.

Many Hindus see no contradiction in honoring several deities. A common teaching, drawn from a Rig Veda verse, holds that truth is one, though the wise call it by many names. Some Hindus understand the deities as many faces of one divine reality. Others worship one supreme God and see the other deities as powerful beings under that God.

a descent; a form in which a deity, especially Vishnu, comes to earth

lessons.title: Shiva, Devi and Ganesha
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus worship Shiva or the Goddess, Devi, as supreme, and nearly all honor Ganesha as the remover of obstacles.
reading: A famous bronze sculpture from South India shows *Shiva* dancing inside a ring of flames. One foot stands on a small figure representing ignorance. One hand holds a drum, the sound of creation. Another holds fire, the force of destruction. Shiva's worshipers, called Shaivas, see him as the supreme God who creates, preserves and destroys in an endless cosmic dance. He is also pictured as a great yogi meditating on a mountain.

Other Hindus center their worship on the Goddess, often called *Devi* or Shakti, meaning divine power. Her followers are called Shaktas. She takes many forms. Durga rides a lion and defeats a buffalo demon. Kali, dark and fierce, destroys evil and ego. Lakshmi brings good fortune, and Saraswati brings learning and music. For Shaktas, the Goddess is the supreme power behind the universe.

*Ganesha*, with his elephant head, is honored by nearly all Hindus, whatever deity they worship most. In one well-known story, he is the son of Shiva and the goddess Parvati. He is called the remover of obstacles, so many Hindus pray to him before starting anything new: a trip, an exam, a wedding or a business. His image often stands near the doorway of homes and temples.

These traditions overlap. A family may keep images of Ganesha, Krishna and Durga on the same shelf. Some Hindus, called Smartas, worship several deities as equal forms of the one Brahman. The tradition makes room for devotion to one chosen deity while respecting others.

lessons.title: Four Paths to the Goal
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu teachers describe several paths, or yogas, toward moksha: knowledge, devotion, selfless action and meditation.
reading: Four people might all be walking toward the same goal. One sits with a teacher, studying the Upanishads and asking who she truly is. One sings devotional songs to Krishna every evening. One runs a free clinic and tries to work without seeking praise. One wakes before dawn to sit still and quiet the mind. Hindu tradition would say all four are practicing *yoga*, a word that means joining or discipline.

The path of knowledge is *jnana yoga*. It uses study, reflection and insight to see through ignorance and recognize the true self. It is closely tied to the Upanishads and to Advaita teachers such as Shankara. A student on this path might ask, again and again, who am I, and set aside every answer that names only the body or the mind.

The path of devotion is *bhakti yoga*: love and surrender to a personal God. Bhakti movements spread across India from about the 6th century CE onward, carried by poet-saints who sang in everyday languages instead of Sanskrit. The 16th-century poet Mirabai, a devotee of Krishna, is still sung today. Bhakti is the most widely practiced path. The path of action is *karma yoga*: doing one's duty without selfish attachment to results, a teaching at the heart of the Bhagavad Gita.

The path of meditation is often called raja yoga, the royal path. It trains the body, breath and mind to reach deep stillness. It draws on the Yoga Sutras attributed to Patanjali. Many Hindus see these paths as suited to different temperaments, and most mix them. The Gita itself teaches all of them.

lessons.title: Puja at Home and in the Temple
lessons.mainIdea: Puja is Hindu worship through offerings of light, flowers, food and prayer, performed at home shrines and in temples.
reading: Early in the morning, a woman in a Chicago suburb bathes, then stands before a small shrine in her kitchen. She lights a lamp and a stick of incense. She offers a flower and a little rice to an image of Ganesha, and quietly recites a prayer. This takes five minutes. It is *puja*, worship through offerings, and in many Hindu homes it happens every day.

In a temple, puja is larger. A priest bathes, dresses and adorns the *murti*, the sacred image of the deity. Many Hindus believe the deity is truly present in the murti once it has been consecrated. During arati, the priest waves a lamp in circles before the image while worshipers sing. Food offered to the deity is then shared among worshipers as *prasad*, a blessed gift. Worshipers remove their shoes before entering, as a sign of respect.

The Bhagavad Gita offers a line many Hindus quote about puja: Krishna says that whoever offers him even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. The point is the love behind the offering, not its cost. This helps explain why puja can be simple or grand.

Hindu temples are called mandirs. The Chicago area has many, including the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago in Lemont and the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora. For many families in the United States, the temple is also a community center with language classes, dance lessons and festival meals.

lessons.title: Diwali and Holi
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali, the festival of lights, and Holi, the spring festival of colors, are among the most widely celebrated Hindu holidays, each with several stories behind it.
reading: Hindu festivals follow a lunar calendar, so their dates on the Western calendar shift each year. *Diwali* usually falls in October or November, on the new moon of the month of Kartik. It lasts about five days. Families clean their homes, light rows of diyas, set off fireworks, share sweets and wear new clothes. Many worship Lakshmi, goddess of good fortune, and many business owners begin a new account book.

Diwali carries several stories. In northern India, many remember Rama's return to Ayodhya after his exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana. In parts of South India, many recall Krishna's defeat of the demon Narakasura. The shared theme is light overcoming darkness and good overcoming evil. Jains observe Diwali as the day their teacher Mahavira reached liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas on the same days.

*Holi* comes in early spring, on the full moon of the month of Phalguna. On the night before, many communities light bonfires recalling the story of Prahlad, a young devotee of Vishnu saved from the fire, while his wicked aunt Holika burned. The next morning, people throw colored powder and water at each other in the streets. Many connect the colors to Krishna's playful youth.

For a day, Holi loosens social rules. Old and young, rich and poor, may all end up covered in pink and green. In Chicago, Holi gatherings at temples, parks and universities often welcome people of any background, and many non-Hindu students join in the colors.

lessons.title: Caste: History and Reform
lessons.mainIdea: Caste is a system of inherited social groups in South Asia; Hindus and reformers have long debated it, and India's Constitution outlawed untouchability in 1950.
reading: Caste is one of the most debated subjects in the study of Hinduism, and it should be described carefully. Ancient Hindu texts describe four varnas, or classes (each one a *varna*): Brahmins, priests and teachers; Kshatriyas, rulers and warriors; Vaishyas, merchants and farmers; and Shudras, laborers and servants. One Rig Veda hymn pictures these classes coming from different parts of a cosmic being. In practice, daily life was organized by thousands of smaller birth groups, each called a *jati*, often tied to an occupation and a region.

Over centuries, some groups were placed outside the varnas and treated as untouchable. They faced exclusion from temples, wells and schools. Many members of these communities today use the name *Dalit*, meaning broken or oppressed, as a name of dignity and protest. Caste also affected other religious communities in South Asia, not only Hindus.

Criticism of caste is old. Many bhakti poet-saints taught that God welcomes every devotee, whatever their birth. In the 19th and 20th centuries, reformers pushed harder. Gandhi campaigned against untouchability. B. R. Ambedkar, a Dalit lawyer and scholar, fought caste discrimination, chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution, and in 1956 converted to Buddhism with a large number of followers. The Constitution, adopted in 1950, abolished untouchability and banned caste discrimination.

Today caste is still a live issue. Many Hindus say it is a social custom, not a core religious teaching, and point to the Upanishads' claim that the same atman lives in every being. Others argue that religious texts helped support the system. Caste discrimination has also become a public issue in some American workplaces and universities. A fair student of religion describes both the history and the reform.

chapters.bigQuestion: What should a person do when duty and conscience seem to point in different directions?

story.title: The Chariot Between the Armies
story.kicker: On the morning of a great battle, the finest archer in India sets down his bow and refuses to fight.
paragraphs: Conch shells blare across a wide plain called Kurukshetra, in northern India. Two enormous armies face each other: elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers stretching to the horizon. On one side stand the five Pandava brothers and their allies. On the other stand their cousins, the Kauravas, who cheated the Pandavas out of their kingdom. After years of exile and failed peace talks, the war is about to begin.

Arjuna, the third Pandava brother and the greatest archer of his age, turns to his charioteer. Drive me out between the two armies, he says, so I can see who I am fighting. The charioteer is Krishna, his friend and cousin. Krishna has promised not to fight in this war, only to drive Arjuna's chariot. He guides the white horses into the open ground between the lines and stops.

Arjuna looks across. He sees Bhishma, the great-uncle who helped raise him. He sees Drona, the teacher who taught him to shoot. He sees cousins, uncles, the sons of friends. His mouth goes dry. His skin burns. His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. What good is a kingdom, he asks, if I must kill my own family to win it? He sinks down onto the seat of the chariot, his eyes full of tears, and says he will not fight.

Everything stops. And in that pause, according to the Mahabharata, Krishna begins to speak. His answer, and the conversation that follows, fills eighteen short chapters. Hindus call it the Bhagavad Gita, the Song of the Lord. Many Hindus revere Krishna as God himself, an avatar of Vishnu, speaking to a frightened human being.

Readers have argued about this conversation for more than two thousand years. Is it about a real war, or about the battle inside every person? Does it support fighting, or teach a deeper peace? Philosophers, priests, poets, American writers and Mohandas Gandhi have all turned to it. This chapter reads the Gita in its setting, follows Krishna's teaching and meets some of its many readers.
story.think: Arjuna faces a choice between two duties: to his family and to his role as a warrior. What would you want to know before advising him?

lessons.title: The Mahabharata in Outline
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata is a vast Sanskrit epic about a family war; the Bhagavad Gita is one short part of it.
reading: The *Mahabharata* is one of the longest poems ever composed. In its fullest versions it runs to about 100,000 couplets, many times longer than Homer's Iliad and Odyssey together. Tradition names the sage Vyasa as its author. Scholars think it grew over many centuries, roughly from 400 BCE to 400 CE, as generations of storytellers added to it. It belongs to the smriti texts, the remembered tradition.

At its heart is a quarrel between cousins. The five Pandava brothers, sons of King Pandu, are rivals of the hundred Kaurava brothers, led by Duryodhana, son of the blind king Dhritarashtra. In a rigged game of dice, the Pandavas lose everything, including their kingdom. Their shared wife, Draupadi, is dragged before the court and humiliated. The Pandavas are sent into exile for thirteen years.

When they return, Duryodhana refuses to give back even five villages. Both sides gather allies, and the war at Kurukshetra lasts eighteen days. Nearly every warrior dies. The Pandavas win, but the victory is full of grief. The epic asks hard questions about dharma: what is right when every choice causes harm?

The *Bhagavad Gita* sits in the sixth of the epic's eighteen books, just before the fighting begins. It has 700 verses in eighteen chapters. Because so many Hindus treat it as scripture on its own, it is often printed and read by itself, apart from the larger epic.

lessons.title: The Ramayana in Outline
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana tells of Prince Rama, his exile and his rescue of Sita, and it presents a model of dharma that millions of Hindus love.
reading: The *Ramayana*, credited to the poet Valmiki, is shorter than the Mahabharata but still long: about 24,000 couplets. Its hero is *Rama*, prince of the city of Ayodhya, whom many Hindus worship as an avatar of Vishnu. Just before Rama is to be crowned, a promise his father once made to a queen forces the king to send Rama into exile for fourteen years. Rama goes without complaint, because obeying his father is his dharma.

His wife, *Sita*, and his brother Lakshmana choose to go with him. In the forest, the demon king Ravana of Lanka kidnaps Sita. Rama searches for her with the help of Hanuman, a devoted and powerful monkey hero, and an army of monkeys and bears. They build a bridge to Lanka, defeat Ravana and rescue Sita. Rama returns home and is crowned, and the city is lit with lamps.

For many Hindus, Rama is the ideal son, husband and king, and Sita is a model of loyalty and courage. The epic also raises hard questions. After the rescue, Rama makes Sita prove her faithfulness by walking through fire, and in some versions he later sends her away because of public gossip. Hindus, including many Hindu women writers, have discussed and debated these scenes for centuries.

The Ramayana exists in many versions. The 16th-century poet Tulsidas retold it in Hindi as the Ramcharitmanas, still recited daily in many homes. Versions spread across Southeast Asia, including Thailand and Indonesia. Hanuman became a beloved figure of devotion in his own right.

lessons.title: Epics as Living Stories
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus meet the epics less often by reading them than through performance, festival, song, film and television.
reading: Each autumn, in towns across northern India, a stage goes up in an open field. For ten nights, local actors perform the Ram Lila, the play of Rama, scene by scene. On the tenth day, the festival of *Dussehra*, huge paper figures of Ravana, stuffed with fireworks, are set alight while crowds cheer. The story ends where Diwali begins: Rama's return home a few weeks later.

Most Hindus first learn the epics this way: from grandparents, festivals, temple dance, comic books and film. In 1987 and 1988, a television series of the Ramayana aired weekly on India's national channel. Accounts from the time describe streets emptying while it played, and some families garlanding their television sets. A Mahabharata series followed. Both have been rebroadcast many times.

This matters for how we study these texts. An *oral tradition* keeps a story alive through telling, singing and acting, not only through a book. The same scene can be performed differently in Kerala and in Bengal, in Bali and in Chicago. When scholars say the epics are living texts, they mean that each retelling is part of the tradition, not a copy of it.

In the Chicago area, temples and cultural groups hold Ram Lila performances and Dussehra celebrations, and children learn the epics in weekend classes. For many families in the diaspora, these stories are a way of passing on language, values and identity.

lessons.title: The Frame of the Gita
lessons.mainIdea: The Gita is told as a report to a blind king, and it opens with Arjuna's collapse as he sees his own family on the other side.
reading: The Gita does not begin with Krishna or Arjuna. It begins with a question from the blind king *Dhritarashtra*, father of the Kauravas, who is far from the battlefield. His advisor Sanjaya has been granted divine sight, so he can see and hear everything at Kurukshetra. The king asks what his sons and the sons of Pandu are doing on the field of dharma. Sanjaya's answer is the whole Gita.

This frame matters. The king is literally blind, and many readers see his blindness as a symbol of his refusal to see that his sons are in the wrong. Sanjaya, by contrast, sees clearly. The story reminds readers that the Gita is a report, told within a story, told within a larger epic.

The first chapter describes the armies, then Arjuna's despair. He lists the kinds of harm war will bring: families destroyed, traditions lost, social order broken. He argues that killing his teachers and relatives would be a grave wrong, even if they are the aggressors. Arjuna's reasons are serious ones. He is not only afraid; he is thinking about ethics.

Arjuna is also a *kshatriya*, a member of the warrior class, whose dharma in the epic is to protect the people and fight a righteous war. So he is caught between two claims of dharma: his duty to his family and his duty as a warrior. The Gita is the answer to that dilemma. Chapter 1 ends with Arjuna sitting down in the chariot, his bow cast aside.

lessons.title: The Self That Cannot Be Slain
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna first answers Arjuna's grief by teaching that the true self, the atman, is eternal and is not destroyed when the body dies.
reading: Krishna's first response is sharp. He tells Arjuna to shake off this weakness and stand up. Then his tone changes, and he begins to teach. The wise, he says, do not grieve for the living or the dead. Why? Because the real self, the *atman*, was never born and will never die. Bodies come and go, but the self that lives in them is eternal.

Krishna compares death to changing clothes. As a person throws away worn-out garments and puts on new ones, the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones. This is the Upanishads' teaching about atman and samsara, now spoken on a battlefield. Arjuna's grief, Krishna argues, rests on a mistake: confusing the body with the self.

Krishna then adds a second argument, from dharma. For a kshatriya, he says, nothing is better than a righteous war. To walk away would bring dishonor and would abandon his duty. Readers have long noticed that these two arguments work on different levels. One is about the eternal nature of the self. The other is about Arjuna's role in society.

Many readers find this teaching troubling as well as comforting. Can it be used to excuse violence? Hindu teachers have answered in different ways, and later lessons show how Gandhi read these verses. What is clear is that the Gita presents the self as something no weapon can touch.

words.d: the true, eternal self in each being, which the Gita teaches is never born and never dies
living in a body; the Gita speaks of the self as embodied in one body after another

lessons.title: Action Without Attachment
lessons.mainIdea: The Gita's most famous teaching is to act according to one's duty while letting go of attachment to the results.
reading: Think of a doctor who gives every patient her best effort. Some recover and some do not. If she measured herself only by results, she might burn out, or cut corners to protect her record. The Gita offers another way. In chapter 2, Krishna tells Arjuna that he has a right to his action, but never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, he says, and do not cling to doing nothing.

This is the heart of *karma yoga*, the path of action. Krishna does not tell Arjuna to withdraw from the world. He tells him to act, and to act well, but without selfish desire for a particular outcome. The Gita calls this *nishkama karma*, desireless action. Krishna says that yoga is evenness of mind in success and failure, and also that yoga is skill in action.

Why does this matter? In Hindu thought, action done from selfish desire binds a person to karma and rebirth. Action done without attachment, as an offering to God, does not bind. So the Gita turns ordinary work into a spiritual path. A farmer, a parent, a soldier or a student can walk toward liberation through daily duties.

The Gita also warns against doing someone else's duty. It is better, Krishna says, to do one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well. Readers debate how to apply this. Some see it as support for traditional roles. Others read it as a call to find and do one's true work.

lessons.title: Devotion and the Vision of God
lessons.mainIdea: In the Gita's later chapters Krishna reveals himself as the supreme God and teaches that loving devotion, bhakti, is the surest path.
reading: In chapter 11, Arjuna asks to see Krishna's divine form. Krishna grants him divine sight. Arjuna then sees the *vishvarupa*, the universal form: countless faces, arms and eyes, blazing like a thousand suns, holding all the worlds and all the gods. He sees the warriors of both armies rushing into Krishna's mouths. Terrified, Arjuna begs to see his friend's familiar human form again, and Krishna returns to it.

This vision shows what many Hindus believe about Krishna: that the friendly charioteer is the supreme God, source and end of all things. It also shows how overwhelming the divine can be. After the vision, the Gita's tone grows warmer. Krishna says that those who worship him with love are dear to him, and that he quickly lifts them out of the ocean of death and rebirth.

This is *bhakti*, loving devotion. The Gita teaches that anyone can take this path, whatever their birth, gender or learning. Near the end, in chapter 18, Krishna gives what many devotees call his final word: let go of all other duties, take refuge in me alone, and I will free you from all wrongs; do not grieve.

The Gita does not reject the paths of knowledge and action. It weaves them together: know the eternal self, act without attachment, and offer everything to God with love. Different schools weigh the three differently. Devotional movements such as the Vaishnava traditions often see bhakti as the crown of the Gita.

loving devotion to a personal God

lessons.title: The Person of Steady Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: The Gita describes an ideal person whose mind stays calm and steady, free from craving, fear and anger, while still acting in the world.
reading: Arjuna asks a practical question in chapter 2: how does a person of steady wisdom speak, sit and walk? Krishna's answer paints a portrait of the *sthitaprajna*, the one whose wisdom is steady. Such a person is not shaken by sorrow and does not crave pleasure. Fear and anger have fallen away. Success and failure, praise and blame, leave the mind level.

Krishna uses two images. Such a person draws the senses back from their objects, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. And such a person is like the ocean: rivers pour into it from every side, yet it stays within its shores. Desires still arise, but they do not overflow the mind.

Krishna also explains how a mind falls apart. Dwelling on things creates attachment. Attachment breeds desire, and desire, when blocked, turns to anger. Anger clouds judgment, and confused judgment ruins a person. This chain of cause and effect is one of the Gita's best-known psychological teachings.

Notice that the steady person is not someone who has left the world. Arjuna is still asked to fight, and householders are still asked to work. The Gita's ideal is *equanimity*, inner calm, joined to action. Many modern readers, Hindu and not, value this part of the Gita for dealing with stress and pressure.

sections.title: The Gita in the Modern World

lessons.title: Gandhi and the Gita
lessons.mainIdea: Mohandas Gandhi called the Gita his guide and read its battlefield as the inner struggle of every person, drawing from it a teaching of selfless, nonviolent action.
reading: As a young law student in London in the late 1880s, Mohandas Gandhi was invited by two English friends to read the Gita with them. They read Edwin Arnold's translation, The Song Celestial. Gandhi later wrote that he was embarrassed to have not yet read it in Sanskrit or Gujarati. The book became central to his life. He called it his mother and turned to it whenever he faced doubt.

Gandhi did not read the Gita as approval of war. He read the battle at Kurukshetra as an *allegory*, a story in which characters and events stand for deeper meanings. For him, the war was the struggle inside every human heart between good and evil impulses. The Pandavas and Kauravas were forces within the self. Krishna was the voice of truth guiding the person.

From the Gita's teaching of action without attachment, Gandhi drew his idea of selfless service. He translated the Gita into Gujarati, his native language, with commentary he titled Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment. Joined with *ahimsa*, nonviolence, this reading shaped his method of *satyagraha*, holding firmly to truth through nonviolent resistance.

Not all readers agree with Gandhi. Some Hindu thinkers of his time, such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, read the Gita as a call to energetic action in the world, including political struggle against British rule. Scholars note that the text itself is set on a real battlefield. The Gita's openness to both readings is part of why it has mattered to so many people.

lessons.title: Many Readers, Many Readings
lessons.mainIdea: For more than a thousand years, teachers, translators and writers in India and the West have read the Gita in strikingly different ways.
reading: Hindu philosophers have written *commentaries* on the Gita for centuries. The 8th-century teacher Shankara read it through Advaita: knowledge of the one Brahman is the key to liberation. The teacher Ramanuja, around the 11th and 12th centuries, read it as a text of devotion to a personal God. Each found his own school's teaching in the same 700 verses.

The Gita reached the English-speaking world in 1785, when Charles Wilkins, working in India, published the first English translation. American writers soon took notice. Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau both read it. In Walden, published in 1854, Thoreau wrote about bathing his mind each morning in the philosophy of the Gita. Edwin Arnold's poetic translation followed in 1885.

In 1893, the Hindu monk *Swami Vivekananda* spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, opening with the words Sisters and Brothers of America. He drew on the Gita and the Upanishads to present Hindu ideas to American audiences. Later teachers brought the Gita to new groups. In 1966, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness in New York, which spread a devotional reading of the Gita worldwide.

Today the Gita is read in schools, temples, business books and hospitals. Hindus recite it at funerals and in daily prayer. Its many readings show the point this course made in unit 1: every translation and commentary is also an *interpretation*, shaped by its reader's time and tradition.

lessons.title: Yoga: Roots and Modern Forms
lessons.mainIdea: Yoga began as a set of Indian spiritual disciplines aimed at liberation; modern yoga, focused on postures and health, grew from those roots in the last 150 years.
reading: Walk into a yoga class at a Chicago gym, and you will see mats, stretching and breathing exercises. The teacher may say namaste at the end. Most people there are not thinking about moksha. Yet the word yoga comes from Indian religious traditions, where it meant a discipline that joins a person to the divine or frees the self.

A key early text is the *Yoga Sutras* attributed to the sage Patanjali, compiled roughly 2,000 years ago, though dates vary. It defines yoga as stilling the movements of the mind. It lays out eight limbs, or steps: ethical restraints such as nonviolence and truthfulness, personal disciplines, posture, breath control, withdrawing the senses, concentration, meditation and *samadhi*, complete absorption. Postures are only one limb, and in Patanjali they mostly mean a steady seat for meditation.

Later *hatha yoga* texts, from around the 11th to 15th centuries, developed more physical postures and breathing methods. In the late 1800s and 1900s, Indian teachers adapted yoga for modern audiences. Vivekananda's book Raja Yoga (1896) presented meditation to Western readers. The teacher T. Krishnamacharya and his students, including B. K. S. Iyengar, developed the posture-based styles now practiced worldwide.

Modern yoga raises questions. Some Hindu groups ask that yoga's Hindu roots be acknowledged, not erased. Some Christian parents have objected to yoga in schools, and courts have looked at whether particular school programs were religious. The United Nations declared June 21 the International Day of Yoga in 2014. The history shows a practice that is both ancient and constantly changing.

choices: It grew from older roots through Indian teachers of the 1800s and 1900s such as Krishnamacharya and Iyengar
It is described in full in the Rig Veda
It was invented in Chicago in 1893
It has no connection to Indian traditions
check.why: Modern posture-based yoga was shaped by teachers such as Krishnamacharya and Iyengar, building on hatha yoga and older traditions.

review.q: What is the setting of the Bhagavad Gita?
choices: Rama's palace in Ayodhya
A temple in Varanasi
A chariot between two armies at Kurukshetra, just before the battle
A forest hermitage where Arjuna studies the Vedas
review.why: The Gita takes place on Arjuna's chariot between the armies at Kurukshetra, within the Mahabharata.

review.q: Who is Krishna in the Gita?
choices: Arjuna's older brother and the eldest Pandava
Arjuna's charioteer, whom many Hindus worship as an avatar of Vishnu
The demon king of Lanka
The poet who wrote the Ramayana
review.why: Krishna drives Arjuna's chariot and, for many Hindus, is God as an avatar of Vishnu.

review.q: Which teaching is central to karma yoga in the Gita?
choices: Act according to your duty without attachment to the results
Avoid all action to escape karma
Seek wealth first, then duty
Leave your family and live in the forest
review.why: Karma yoga means doing one's duty without selfish attachment to its fruits (Gita 2.47).

review.q: Which epic tells the story of Rama, Sita and Hanuman?
choices: The Mahabharata
The Upanishads
The Yoga Sutras
The Ramayana
review.why: The Ramayana, credited to Valmiki, tells of Rama, Sita and Hanuman. The Mahabharata tells of the Pandavas.

review.q: In Arnold's translation of Gita 2.20, what claim does the verse make?
choices: The spirit is born with the body and dies with it
The spirit is birthless, deathless and changeless
Only warriors have a spirit
The spirit lives only in temples
review.why: Arnold's verse says the spirit was never born and will never cease; death does not touch it.

review.q: What does Arjuna see in chapter 11?
choices: Sita walking through fire
The dice game
Krishna's universal form
Vivekananda in Chicago
review.why: In chapter 11 Krishna reveals his universal form, the vishvarupa, to Arjuna.

review.q: How did Gandhi's reading of the Gita shape his public life?
choices: He read the battle as an inner struggle and drew from the Gita a teaching of selfless, nonviolent action
He used it to argue for joining a war against Britain
He rejected it as irrelevant
He read it only as a history of ancient India
review.why: Gandhi read Kurukshetra as an allegory and joined the Gita's non-attachment to nonviolence in satyagraha.

review.q: What do the many commentaries and translations of the Gita show?
choices: That there is only one correct reading
That the Gita was first written in English
That the Gita is read only by priests
That every translation and commentary is also an interpretation
review.why: From Shankara to Gandhi to modern translators, readers have found different meanings, showing that every reading interprets.
